items.title: Does Multi-Agent Collaboration Reduce Hallucination in Clinical Tasks?
items.abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems improve performance on clinical tasks, and that improvement is often read as evidence of a more trustworthy system. However, the two are not the same claim. A clinician acts on the stated reasoning and not only on the conclusion, so whether collaboration reduces hallucination, and what decides when it does, has to be measured in the reasoning too. Yet most evaluations score only the final answer. We evaluate four systems (a single-LLM baseline and three multi-agent topologies) across four models and three clinical tasks, scoring hallucination, under a factuality and faithfulness taxonomy, inside the rationale each system generates and reporting it alongside the task metric. We report that collaboration buys task performance but not lower hallucination as a rule, and no topology is reliably better than another. The effect differs by model: of the $36$ model--system--task comparisons, $12$ are large enough to resolve --- four decreases and eight increases, with no model on both sides. What sets the level, and the direction of any change, is the model rather than the topology or the number of agents. A self-correction experiment is consistent with this: shown its own flagged errors, every model except Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct reduces hallucination; the one model for which collaboration lowers hallucination gains the most, and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, the model whose hallucination it amplifies most, does not reduce its hallucination at all. We find that collaboration redistributes what its models can already do; it does not supply what they cannot.

items.title: Does Private Equity Hurt or Improve Healthcare Value? New Evidence and Mechanisms
items.abstract: What is the impact of private equity (PE) ownership on healthcare value? Does PE ownership reduce healthcare value, and if so, can its effect be mitigated using health information technologies (IT)? Given the significant investments by PE firms in the healthcare sector in recent years, it is increasingly important for stakeholders, including policy makers, care providers, and patients, to understand their likely impact and whether PE ownership is aligned with their interests. Because PE firms seek to improve efficiency and generate short-term financial returns, the cost-cutting strategies used to achieve these goals may come at the expense of care quality, leading to competing hypotheses on the impact of PE ownership on healthcare value. We argue that IT-enabled health information sharing capabilities can help PE-owned hospitals to better manage this cost-quality tension and achieve higher healthcare value. Using a staggered difference-in-differences approach and data from US hospitals from 2008 to 2020, we estimate changes in healthcare value following PE acquisition and ownership. Overall, we find that PE ownership of hospitals reduces healthcare value. This decline is partially driven by reduction in clinical staffing following PE ownership. We further find that pre-existing, hospital health information sharing capabilities mitigate the negative impact of PE ownership on healthcare value. Specifically, such capabilities can strengthen the effect of PE ownership on cost reduction and, at the same time, mitigate PE-induced, care quality deterioration. Our results highlight the critical role of common data standards needed to promote IT-enabled information sharing between healthcare providers, which, in turn, can align the incentives of PE firms with the goals of value-based care.

items.title: DStill: Trajectory Consistency Distillation for Accelerated One-Step Drafting in Block Diffusion Speculative Decoding
items.abstract: Block-diffusion speculative decoding accelerates large language model inference by drafting multiple tokens in parallel. However, one-step drafting in discrete diffusion is limited by token factorization error: each token is predicted from the same masked block, without conditioning on the tokens selected at other positions in that step. This can produce inconsistent drafts and reduce acceptance length. Iterative refinement mitigates this limitation by conditioning later predictions on previously committed tokens, though additional passes increase drafting cost. To address this trade-off between draft fidelity and inference latency, we introduce DStill, a two-stage framework that distills a target-conditioned drafter's own multi-step refinement into one-step drafting. We first train the drafter to complete partially revealed blocks, then use its refinement trajectories to train a student to predict the final completion in one pass. Using a curriculum that gradually transitions from partial to fully masked inputs, we successfully transfer the multi-step refinement capabilities into one step. Across reasoning, math, code benchmarks on three model families DStill improves acceptance length by up to 28% and speedup by up to 25% over one-step DFlash, achieving up to 6.45x speedup over auto-regressive decoding.

items.title: Early and visible detection of fugitive methane leaks in industrial infrared videos via local-global contrast enhancement
items.abstract: Early visualization of greenhouse gases and volatile organic compounds is essential for emission control and industrial safety. Infrared optical gas imaging sequences are difficult to interpret because plumes occupy little of each frame. In our data, mean plume coverage was 6.12%, mean local contrast was 8.09%, and over 72% of samples had local contrast below 10%. We develop an artificial intelligence framework for infrared methane-plume enhancement and early leak detection. It embeds a Local Perception Enhancement Module in a U-shaped Transformer and combines differentiable local contrast limiting, spatial gating, and residual fusion. The study used 180,000 infrared frames from controlled releases and an operating chemical industrial park. The framework achieved a region-of-interest peak signal-to-noise ratio of 35.41 dB and a global structural similarity index of 0.951. Structural ablation confirmed gains in local and global fidelity, structural similarity, and contrast. With a fixed one-stage object detector, enhanced inputs increased mean intersection over union from 76% to 85% and reduced false negatives by 31.5%. For controlled releases of 80 to 4000 mL per minute, enhancement lowered the flow rate at which probability of detection reached 0.9 from 1000 to 300 mL per minute. At two field sites, stable detection occurred 10.5 and 11.8 s earlier. These results connect artificial intelligence-based image enhancement to measurable gains in industrial methane-leak monitoring.

items.title: Early Exposure to Artificial Intelligence in Medical Education: A Knowledge, Attitude and Practice Study among Preclinical Medical Students from Mangaluru, India
items.abstract: Introduction: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is the study of machines that learn from collected data and use human-like reasoning. AI applications are already used in healthcare, and there is a need to understand the need for AI training in the medical curriculum. Aim: To assess the Knowledge, Attitudes, and Practices (KAP) related to AI among first- and second-year MBBS students. Materials and Methods: This cross-sectional study was conducted at AJ Institute of Medical Sciences and Research Centre, Mangaluru, Karnataka, India from April to May 2026, among first- and second-year MBBS students via an online questionnaire; the sample size was 327. Based on existing KAP studies, the questionnaire collected data on AI knowledge (e.g., AI/ML concepts and applications), attitudes (e.g., beliefs about fostering AI knowledge despite its future application), and AI application. Categorical associations were analysed using Chisquare tests. Statistical significance was set at p-value <0.05. Results: Of 327 survey participants, 204 (62.39%) were firstyear medical students. Most reported at least basic knowledge of AI; however, few had prior training {26 (7.95%) attended AI workshops, and 41 (12.54%) received curriculum training}. Most students believed medical schools should teach AI concepts (269, 82.26%) and supported incorporating AI into the curriculum (193, 59.02%). ChatGPT was the most popular AI tool, used by 315 (96.33%) respondents, primarily for exam preparation and studying, with other uses less frequent. The key obstacles included insufficient knowledge/lack of proper training in AI (222, 67.89%) and concerns about data privacy and ethical issues (157,48.01%). Conclusion: Despite extensive exposure to AI (as most students used AI tools), students had limited knowledge or training in it. Students were optimistic about AI in healthcare and strongly supported AI education. These results suggest incorporating AI training into the medical curriculum to bridge knowledge gaps and meet learners’ needs.

items.title: Economic Turbulence and Organizational AI Use in MSMEs: The Competing Roles of Perceived Benefits and Risks
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) may support adaptation in micro-, small-, and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs) facing economic uncertainty. This study examines a dual-pathway appraisal framework using a cross-sectional survey of 537 respondents reporting on Chinese MSMEs already using AI. The outcome represents the extent of organizational AI use rather than initial adoption or continuance intention. Confirmatory factor analysis and latent-variable structural equation modeling were conducted with 5000 case-bootstrap resamples. The specification adds familiarity–appraisal paths and a benefit–risk residual covariance. Economic turbulence was positively associated with perceived benefits, which were positively associated with AI use. The specific indirect association through benefits was significant (B = 0.058, 95% CI [0.013, 0.118]), whereas the risk-mediated association was not. Perceived risks were negatively associated with AI use. Familiarity was positively associated with use and risks, but its association with benefits was nonsignificant. The direct turbulence–use association was nonsignificant; the total association was positive and significant (B = 0.209, 95% CI [0.047, 0.371]). The model explained 70.6% of the variance in AI use (CFI = 0.997; RMSEA = 0.014; SRMR = 0.021). The findings identify asymmetric appraisal associations among existing AI users; the cross-sectional design does not establish causal ordering.

items.title: Effect of a Health Education Program on the Prevention of Work-Related Musculoskeletal Disorders on School Teachers’ Knowledge
items.abstract: Background: Physical and occupational demands of teachers due to their profession exposed them various ergonomic risk factors, making them particularly vulnerable to musculoskeletal disorders (MSDs).This study assessed the effect of a health education program on the prevention of work-related musculoskeletal disorders on school teachers' knowledge.Method: A quasi-experimental study using a one-group pre-and post-test design was implemented at four primary institutes located within the El Mansoura Azharian Zone.A total of 46 school teachers agreed to participate in the study.Three data collection tools were used: a socio-demographic and occupational data self-administered questionnaire, a school teachers' knowledge self-administered questionnaire, and teachers' feedback related to the educational program implementation.Results: Reported significant improvements with a large effect size (t=23.88,P≤0.001, d=4.79) in the teachers' knowledge of work-related musculoskeletal disorders, including definitions, types, signs and symptoms, ergonomics, and management from the pre-test to the post-test assessment of the educational program Conclusion and Recommendations: The study found that the work-related musculoskeletal disorders program effectively increased teachers' knowledge regarding musculoskeletal disorders and ergonomics.The study recommends continuing to provide interventions such as occupational health education lectures, on-site ergonomics training, and publicity brochures to enhance teachers' health knowledge regarding work-related musculoskeletal disorders.

items.title: EFL LEARNERS' PERCEPTIONS OF AI TOOLS FOR SPEAKING PRACTICE AND SPEAKING ANXIETY: A PROPOSED SURVEY OF FIRST-YEAR UNIVERSITY STUDENTS IN UZBEKISTAN
items.abstract: This proposed study aims to explore first-year university EFL learners' perceptions of using artificial intelligence (AI) tools, such as conversational AI assistants and pronunciation applications, for English-speaking practice. It focuses on learners' perceived speaking anxiety, perceived usefulness of feedback, and views about the advantages and limitations of AI-supported practice. A questionnaire-based survey is planned with approximately 30 first-year students studying English Language and Literature at Andijan State Institute of Foreign Languages. The questionnaire will include Likert-scale items and a small number of open-ended questions. Quantitative responses will be summarized using descriptive statistics, while open-ended responses will be grouped into recurring themes. Because data have not yet been collected, this proposal does not report empirical findings or claim that AI tools improve speaking performance. The study is intended to provide context-specific preliminary evidence about how students perceive AI-assisted speaking practice and to inform future, larger-scale research.

items.title: EGI-BENCH: An Enterprise General Intelligence Benchmark Suite
items.abstract: Enterprise adoption of LLMs in agentic workflows is gated by evaluations that span a wide arc of abilities: CRM operations, heterogeneous-document retrieval, personal data understanding, multi-turn planning, tool use, function calling, long-horizon research, and long-context software engineering. These evaluations live today in separate repositories with divergent runners, dependencies, and scoring conventions, which makes cross-benchmark comparison difficult and obscures what a single aggregate number actually represents. We release EGI-BENCH, a unified LLM agent benchmark suite that consolidates eight enterprise facing agent benchmarks (CRMARENA, HERB, PERSONABENCH, USERBENCH, MCP-UNIVERSE, MCPEVAL, BENCHFORCE, LOCOBENCH) behind a single command-line interface with two runtime-budgeted execution modes. On top of the suite we define the Enterprise General Intelligence (EGI) Score, a six-dimensional framework (M1-M6) whose buckets are populated by fine-grained sub-metrics routed from each benchmark rather than by benchmark-level averages. We describe the suite, the sub-metric routing, and the quick/deep budgets, and report results for fourteen frontier and cost-efficient LLMs spanning the GPT, Claude, and Gemini families under quick mode. Top-line EGI ranges from 39.6 (GPT-4o mini) to 65.6 (gpt-5.5), and no single model dominates every capability axis: gpt-5.5 leads task outcome, planning, and retrieval grounding; Claude Sonnet 4.5 leads tool actioning and safety/abstention; and Claude Haiku 4.5 leads engineering quality. Code is available at https://github.com/SalesforceAIResearch/egi-bench.

items.title: Emerging AI Era in Education: Achieving a Multifaceted Revolution That Is Sustainable Using AutoML
items.abstract: Recently, ChatGPT’s impressive results on a number of standardized academic assessments have brought artificial intelligence (AI) within the broader discourse surrounding the direction of education. Deep learning has the potential to completely change the way that education is delivered, thus it is critical to comprehend how it will affect the present framework in order to plan for the long-term development and implementation of AI-driven educational technology in colleges and universities. During an examination and evaluation of the body of research, this study seeks to understand how AI may affect education along three main dimensions: applications, benefits, and problems. This article emphasizes the application of AI to automatic evaluation, autonomous tutoring systems, customized instruction, and collaborative teacher–student education. It also discusses the probable drawbacks, moral dilemmas, and future directions for implementing AI in the classroom. In the end, we discover that adopting the new technology while putting in place safeguards to stop its misuse is the only viable course of action.

items.title: Employability Skills in the Modern Labor Market: The Role of Internships and the Development of Technical, Leadership, Digital and Language Competencies
items.abstract: The rapid changes in the global labor market, driven by digital transformation, globalization, technological advancement and artificial intelligence, have significantly changed employers' expectations of university graduates. Academic qualifications alone are no longer sufficient to secure employment, as organizations increasingly seek graduates who possess practical experience and a combination of technical and transferable skills. This paper addresses the importance of internships during university studies and discusses the key skills and competencies required to improve graduate employability in today's competitive labor market through a short review of the literature and related organizations. It highlights internships as an effective bridge between higher education and the workplace by enabling students to apply theoretical knowledge in real organizational settings, gain professional experience, develop workplace confidence and become familiar with organizational culture before graduation. The paper also explores four essential categories of employability skills that are required across different industries: technical skills, leadership and soft skills, computer skills and language skills. These competencies contribute to improving employee performance, organizational effectiveness, career development and long term employability. Furthermore, the paper emphasizes that preparing students for employment is a shared responsibility among universities, employers, policymakers and students. Higher education institutions should integrate internships and practical learning opportunities into academic programs, while employers should strengthen collaboration with universities to ensure that graduates possess the competencies required by the labor market. At the same time, students should continuously develop their professional skills throughout their university studies. The paper concludes that combining internship experience with the continuous development of technical, leadership, digital and language competencies significantly enhance graduates' readiness for employment and supports sustainable career success in an increasingly dynamic and technology driven labor market. It also highlighted the need to do quantitative studies to cover this topic in the middle east.

items.title: Employee AI Use and Readiness in Applied Higher Education: Awareness, Barriers, and HRM Implications
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) adoption in higher education increasingly represents a challenge in workforce development and organizational transformation, rather than a purely technological issue. This study re-analyzed survey data from 311 faculty members, training instructors, and administrative staff at the Public Authority for Applied Education and Training (PAAET), Kuwait, to examine the associations of AI awareness and perceived barriers with AI usage/readiness from a human resource management perspective. AI usage/readiness was treated as a self-reported indicator of AI-related human capital readiness rather than as a measure of demonstrated competence or comprehensive organizational readiness. Ordinal confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modeling were conducted using robust diagonally weighted least squares/weighted least squares mean and variance adjusted (DWLS/WLSMV) estimation. The refined 12-item, three-factor model demonstrated satisfactory reliability and validity, although model fit was mixed across scaled and robust indices. A near-zero eigenvalue also indicated possible numerical instability, warranting cautious interpretation and independent confirmation. AI awareness was strongly and positively associated with usage/readiness (β = 0.782, p < 0.001), whereas perceived barriers showed a small positive adjusted association (β = 0.117, p = 0.019). Together, the predictors explained 66.0% of the variance in usage/readiness. The positive association with perceived barriers may indicate that employees who engage more extensively with AI are more likely to recognize institutional and technical constraints. Building on these findings, this study proposes two conceptual extensions for future validation: a five-level AI capability maturity model for higher education and a seven-domain AI-enhanced instructor competency framework. The findings emphasize the need to integrate employee capability, institutional support, responsible AI governance, and continuous learning to develop sustainable AI readiness. Given the cross-sectional, self-reported design, these findings should be interpreted as associations rather than causal effects.

items.title: Employees' Justice Perceptions and Trust in AI Systems for Performance Evaluation: Uncovering the Role of Gender and Culture
items.abstract: Organizations are increasingly using artificial intelligence (AI) to support employee performance evaluation, yet employees' perceptions of and responses to these systems within this high-stakes workplace context remain insufficiently understood. Drawing on social exchange, organizational justice, and trust theories, this study examines how employees' justice perceptions shape trust in AI-based performance evaluation systems and how trust in AI relates to broader employee–organization relationship factors, including trust in the organization, trust in managers, and affective commitment. It further investigates whether these relationships vary across gender and Eastern–Western regional contexts. Survey data from 291 employees across Eastern and Western countries were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling and multigroup analysis. The findings show that distributive and procedural justice perceptions positively influence employee trust in AI across regional contexts, with distributive justice exerting the stronger effect. Trust in AI, in turn, positively influences affective commitment in both contexts. Gender differences were observed in the relationship between procedural justice perception and trust in AI within the Eastern sample but not within the Western sample. These findings contribute to research on organizational justice, trust, and AI in organizations, while also offering practical insights for fostering employee trust and supporting effective AI implementation in performance evaluation.

items.title: Engineering Biomacromolecules for Advanced Drug Delivery Through Structure–Function Relationships
items.abstract: Biomacromolecules have emerged as versatile building blocks for advanced drug delivery systems owing to their biocompatibility, biodegradability, chemical functionality, molecular recognition, and capacity for hierarchical organization. However, their delivery performance is governed not simply by material identity but by complex relationships between molecular structure and functional behavior. This review provides a structure–function-oriented overview of biomacromolecular drug delivery, encompassing polysaccharides, proteins and polypeptides, peptides, and nucleic acid-based materials. Particular emphasis is placed on key molecular determinants, including molecular weight and chain architecture, charge and functional groups, hydrophobicity and amphiphilicity, molecular conformation, intermolecular interactions, and biodegradability. We further discuss how chemical modification, crosslinking, self-assembly, targeting, and stimuli-responsive engineering translate these molecular features into functional delivery architectures, including nanoparticles, micelles, nanogels, hydrogels, fibrous matrices, and hybrid systems. The influence of biomacromolecular structure on drug loading, encapsulation, controlled release, protein adsorption, mucosal interactions, cellular uptake, intracellular trafficking, biodistribution, and biocompatibility is critically examined. Representative applications in cancer therapy, nucleic acid delivery, protein and peptide delivery, anti-inflammatory treatment, regenerative medicine, and localized delivery are also highlighted. Finally, current challenges associated with structural heterogeneity, batch-to-batch variability, stability, safety, scale-up, and manufacturing are discussed. Future integration of advanced characterization, molecular modeling, Quality-by-Design, and artificial intelligence/machine learning may enable a transition from empirical formulation toward predictive biomacromolecular engineering. Establishing quantitative links across molecular structure, material properties, carrier architecture, biological interactions, and therapeutic performance will be essential for the rational design and clinical translation of next-generation biomacromolecular drug delivery systems.

items.title: Environmental Pressures and Modelled Health Pathways of Data Centers in the AI Era: A Systematic Review and Evidence Map
items.abstract: Data centers are a critical component of digital infrastructure, and their expansion in the artificial intelligence era raises concerns about environmental pressures and potential implications for human health. This systematic review and evidence map synthesized evidence on data-center-related environmental pressures, exposures and health impacts. Bibliographic databases, Google Scholar, preprint servers, gray literature and citation searching were used to identify eligible studies. Methodological quality was assessed using QualSyst or the JBI checklist, and each result was classified along a four-level pathway from environmental pressure to population exposure, modeled health impact and observed health outcome (PROSPERO CRD420261502966). Thirty-six studies yielding 112 quantitative estimates were included. The most downstream level reached was environmental pressure only in 18 studies (50.0%), population exposure in 12 (33.3%) and modeled health impact in only six (16.7%); no study reached the observed-health-outcome level. Across heterogeneous satellite, modeling, and field-monitoring studies, reported localized temperature differences ranged from 0.35 to 2.07 °C, with preliminary evidence of vegetation loss. Exposure assessment was predominantly model-based (26/36), and all six studies reaching the health-impact level estimated rather than observed health outcomes; four of these six studies were preprints. Environmental pressures attributable to data-center activity have been quantified across multiple domains, but evidence linking these pressures to human health remains limited to modeled health impacts. No included study evaluated observed human-health outcomes using epidemiological or clinical data. Therefore, the current evidence base does not establish whether data-center-related exposures are associated with health effects in exposed populations.

items.title: Epilepsy domain adapted large language models enhance epileptogenic zone prediction from seizure semiology
items.abstract: Seizure semiology provides clinically meaningful clues for localizing the epileptogenic zone (EZ) in drug-resistant focal epilepsy, but its interpretation varies across clinicians and institutions. We aimed to develop and externally validate a domain-adapted large language model for EZ localization from narrative seizure descriptions. We developed EpiSemoLLM using 1,372 surgically verified semiology–EZ pairs collected from 392 published studies and a retrospective cohort from Far Eastern Memorial Hospital. Of these cases, 1,272 were used for model development and 100 were reserved for evaluation. The model combined parameter-efficient fine-tuning with structured epilepsy knowledge and literature-based evidence retrieval. We compared its performance with general-purpose and biomedical language models and with five epileptologists. External validation was conducted in an independent cohort of 83 cases from Taipei Veterans General Hospital evaluated by six epileptologists. Performance was assessed using case-level and region-level localization measures, with uncertainty estimated by paired bootstrap resampling. Here we show that EpiSemoLLM achieves the strongest overall localization performance among the evaluated language models and performs better than the median epileptologist in the held-out cohort. Similar findings are observed in the independent external cohort. The model shows relative strengths in temporal, parietal, occipital, and cingulate localization, whereas clinicians perform better in frontal and insular localization. These findings support the use of domain adaptation and literature-based evidence retrieval for interpreting seizure semiology. EpiSemoLLM may complement clinical reasoning during early presurgical evaluation and help improve the consistency of EZ localization across clinical settings. Prospective validation is needed before routine clinical use. People with epilepsy that does not improve with medicine may be considered for brain surgery. Before surgery, doctors need to identify the part of the brain that is responsible for the seizures and should be targeted during treatment. Signs and symptoms during a seizure can help, but different doctors may interpret them differently. We trained a language model using published reports and hospital records from patients whose seizure-related brain regions had been confirmed by surgery and follow-up. We compared its answers with those of epileptologists and tested it on cases from another hospital. Our model outperformed all baselines and was as accurate as or more accurate than the epileptologists. It is designed to complement clinical expertise and standard presurgical tests, supporting more consistent early assessments. The model outperforms evaluated language models and performs comparably to or better than epileptologists across internal and external cohorts.

items.title: Epistemic reconfiguration in higher education: Generative artificial intelligence, stratification and the renewal of pedagogical judgement
items.abstract: This conceptual article contends that generative artificial intelligence (generative AI) is driving an epistemic reconfiguration in higher education. It places AI within the processes of platformisation through which digital infrastructures reorganise how knowledge is produced, accessed and governed. These changes modify the conditions under which knowledge is recognised and learned, potentially weakening the educational relationship between writing, thinking and understanding when AI use bypasses the cognitive and metacognitive work through which understanding develops. The article develops a framework linking platformisation, AI-mediated meaning-making, and the reorganisation of pedagogy. It argues that these processes produce epistemic stratification by unevenly shaping students’ and institutions’ capacity to sustain epistemic ascent. Artificial intelligence is therefore not merely a technological or assessment challenge, but part of a broader epistemic reconfiguration that reshapes the conditions under which knowledge is produced, recognised and learned. Contribution: Situated in Global South contexts, the article examines how these dynamics intersect with historically entrenched inequalities and forms of epistemic dependency. In response, it advances epistemic ascent, understood as the structured development of conceptual understanding, disciplinary reasoning and judgement, as a central educational objective. The article argues that pedagogical judgement and design-based pedagogies are essential for organising AI use in ways that sustain conceptual engagement, epistemic justice and the university’s public-good mission. The article also illustrates two design-based pedagogical tasks through which lecturers can organise AI-supported learning around conceptual reasoning and disciplinary judgement.

items.title: Evaluating COPD care assistance: a comparative study of ChatGPT-3.5, ChatGPT-4.0, and ERNIE bot performance
items.abstract: Background: Large language model (LLM) chatbots are increasingly used to provide health information, yet their reliability in addressing chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) care questions in the Chinese context remains unclear. To evaluate and compare the performance of three publicly available LLM chatbots - ChatGPT-3.5, ChatGPT-4.0 (OpenAI), and ERNIE Bot (Baidu) - in answering chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) care questions in China. Methods: We performed a cross-sectional comparative evaluation of three publicly available LLM chatbots (ChatGPT-3.5, ChatGPT-4.0, and ERNIE Bot). We developed 40 COPD care questions spanning 7 prespecified domains relevant to patient education and self-management. All questions were submitted in Chinese in independent new chat sessions to minimise context carryover. Three consultant-level respiratory physicians independently rated each response for accuracy (1 = poor, 2 = borderline, 3 = good). We summarised accuracy as the sum of three ratings (range 3-9) and derived a majority-vote accuracy category. For responses rated 'good' by majority vote, physicians additionally rated comprehensiveness on a five-point scale. Information quality was further assessed using a modified DISCERN framework and the Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool (PEMAT) understandability and actionability domains. Results: Most responses were rated as 'good' for accuracy across chatbots. ERNIE Bot achieved higher total accuracy scores than ChatGPT-3.5 and ChatGPT-4.0, and a higher proportion of 'good' ratings in this Chinese-language evaluation. However, comprehensiveness scores for 'good' responses were low across all systems (mean ~ 1.4-2.0/5), and PEMAT actionability was limited, indicating that few responses included concrete, patient-executable steps. Conclusions: Our findings suggest that LLM chatbots may support basic COPD patient education in Chinese settings, but current responses often lack sufficient comprehensiveness and actionable guidance. These tools should not be used as standalone clinical advice and require appropriate safeguards and clinician oversight.

items.title: Evaluating the associations of learning environment with student engagement and learning gains among undergraduate students at a medical university in western China
items.abstract: Introduction As quality improvement in medical education increasingly focuses on the learning processes that students actually experience, it is important to clarify which learning-environment domains are most closely associated with student engagement and how engagement relates to learning gains. Methods In this pooled repeated cross-sectional study, we analyzed 11,717 student responses from four administrations (2021–2024) of the National College Student Survey among undergraduate students at a medical university in western China. The learning environment was assessed across five domains: classroom teaching quality, facilities and resources, developmental support, interpersonal support, and teaching administration. Student engagement was measured across behavioral, emotional, and cognitive dimensions. Learning gains were assessed across six domains. Hierarchical multiple linear regression, cross-sectional indirect association analysis, year-stratified analyses, and k-means clustering were used to examine associations among perceived learning environment, engagement, and learning gains and to explore heterogeneity among students. Results Survey year and background characteristics explained only 1.5–4.0% of the variance in engagement, whereas the five learning-environment domains explained an additional 22.5–27.6%. Classroom teaching quality showed the largest positive associations with behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement, which were statistically significant in every survey wave, and developmental support was also positively associated with all three dimensions. Engagement statistically accounted for 31.93% of the cross-sectional association between perceived learning environment and learning gains (total indirect association = 0.234; total association = 0.734). Person-centered analysis identified a convergent-low profile comprising 37.2% of students, whose scores on perceived learning environment, engagement, and learning gains were all below the sample average; background characteristics were only weakly associated with membership in the three profiles (Cramér’s V ≤ 0.063). Discussion These findings suggest that, in improving educational quality, medical universities should give greater attention to the classroom teaching and developmental support processes that students experience directly in their everyday learning, and should incorporate student engagement and learning experiences into routine, ongoing quality monitoring alongside conventional outcome assessment.

items.title: Evolutionary Dynamics of Feral AI and the Emergence of Digital Ecosystems
items.abstract: The digital world is approaching a profound phase transition, whose primary drivers, we argue, are different from those that dominate current discussions of AI risk. The transition need not begin with a superintelligent system escaping human control, or with an AI acquiring the ability and motivation to reproduce. Rather, we suggest that it may get under way as AI agents routinely delegate tasks by creating or recruiting other agents. As delegation becomes widespread and recursive, vast numbers of agents will be created; inevitably, some will persist, spread, and create others beyond their original tasks and environments. At scale, this changes the rules of the game. Digital environments will become populated by interacting agents that share and compete for computational resources, facilitate or interfere with one another, and face pressures to persist, proliferate, and evade removal. What emerges is an ecology, increasingly shaped not only by what individual agents were designed to do, but also by interactions and selective pressures among them, leading to uncontrolled developments with potentially catastrophic outcomes. While this transition may be difficult to prevent, we identify several dynamics likely to characterize the new digital ecology, which can serve as a basis for understanding the world it may create and perhaps for mitigating some of its consequences.

items.title: Evolving Self-tuning Benchmarks for Long-Horizon Tool Use
items.abstract: For AI assistants to move beyond simple chat interfaces and reliably assist users with applications like Gmail, Venmo, and Slack, we need to improve their tool-use capabilities. However, existing tool use benchmarks are still limited and difficult to scale because they rely on human supervision or are too domain-specific. To make data generation scalable, we propose, TURTLE (Tool Use Related Tasks with Long-Horizon Evolution), an Unsupervised Environment Design (UED) approach to evolve existing tasks using a proposer, a solver, and a feedback generator large language model agents. The proposer is rewarded for difficult yet solvable tasks based on the solver's empirical performance, and the feedback generator summarizes the solver's execution traces for the proposer to exploit. TURTLE produces evolving, self-tuning test suites adaptable to different environment requirements, from supporting user simulators and dense document retrieval to interacting across multiple apps. Empirical results on AppWorld, $τ$-Bench, and AutomationBench using Gemma 4 31B-it show that the evolved tasks target the desired difficulty range (e.g., a 165% increase in the percentage of hard tasks on AppWorld), increase task diversity (in terms of reasoning and simultaneous tool interactions), and elicit a broader range of failure modes than the original tasks.

items.title: Examining Older Adults’ Preferences for Virtual Reality Applications to Support Social and Cognitive Engagement
items.abstract: ObjectiveTo assess older adults' experience, attitudes, and interests toward virtual reality (VR) applications as part of an early phase in the user-centered focused development of the Cognitive Activity Social Technology (CAST) VR system.BackgroundVR offers opportunities to enhance health and well-being in older adults by promoting cognitive, activity, social, and technology engagement. However, limited research has examined older adults' user experience and perceptions.MethodA multi-site study was conducted with 48 community-dwelling older adults aged 65-90. Participants interacted with 16 VR applications through hands-on sessions and first-person video demonstrations. They rated user experience, overall attitudes toward VR, and interest in using VR for various activities.ResultsMost applications were rated as enjoyable, interesting, and easy to use, with minimal reports of physical discomfort. Participants expressed the greatest interest in VR for art, cultural experiences, education, entertainment, and travel, while showing less interest in VR-based social interaction and fitness. Overall, participants found VR technology to be enjoyable and easy to use, but were neutral about VR's usefulness, likely due to the productivity-oriented nature of the usefulness measure.ConclusionThe findings demonstrated the feasibility, usability, and acceptability of VR applications for cognitive and activity engagement among older adults.ApplicationResults highlight the importance of designing VR experiences that align with older adults' preferences and needs. Findings inform user-centered design of VR systems to enhance cognitive engagement, social connectivity, and well-being among older adults.

items.title: Experiences developing structural biology tools with AI coding assistance
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) offer significant potential to accelerate scientific software development, yet their application to structural biology algorithms requires rigorous evaluation. This challenge is examined through the development of xcif, a new native parser for the crystallographic information file (CIF) format, designed to replace a stable but slow parser (ucif) in the Computational Crystallography Toolbox (cctbx). Using an expert-led, artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted workflow, implementation time was reduced from an estimated several months to approximately one week of active human effort. However, this efficiency relied entirely on domain knowledge to specify constraints, intercept plausible but flawed machine-generated code and design adversarial tests. The machine assistance did not replace programming expertise but rather shifted the human engineering burden from writing code to independent validation. Applying the new xcif parser across a corpus of approximately 550 000 archive files confirmed that it produces output identical to both the legacy implementation and GEMMI, a modern high-performance parser. xcif parses roughly an order of magnitude faster than the legacy cctbx parser and 1.3-1.5 times faster than GEMMI, while reducing peak memory use for larger files. This case study demonstrates that AI assistance provides a highly practical, cost-effective pathway for the renewal of mature structural biology infrastructure, provided that the development is strictly governed by expert oversight and objective verification.

items.title: Explainable AI for Criterion-Referenced Oral English Assessment: A Measured Pilot Study
items.abstract: Oral examination is a high-stakes application of artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education, requiring transparency and human oversight. This study presents a pilot AI examiner for university oral English examinations following the IELTS Speaking format. The system combines automatic speech recognition (ASR) using Gemini 2.5 Flash, deterministic extraction of fluency, lexical, syntactic, and semantic indicators, and rubric-constrained assessment using Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite. Low-confidence cases are automatically escalated, and final weighted scores are calculated programmatically, while instructors retain authority over academic decisions. The pilot analyzed 45 spoken responses, of which 26.7% lacked usable word-level timestamps, preventing reliable calculation of temporal indicators and highlighting ASR-related measurement limitations. A post-examination survey collected responses from 67 students, achieving a 62% response rate, to evaluate the internal consistency of composite indices. Comparisons between AI-generated preliminary scores and instructor-released grades across 23 paired sessions revealed near-zero correlations and a pronounced ceiling effect in instructor scores. Consequently, these grades could not serve as a valid criterion for evaluating AI scoring accuracy. Instructor feedback also identified operational challenges requiring refinement. Based on these findings, the study establishes a three-level trust framework grounded in observable pipeline conditions and measured failure frequencies. It also proposes a validation protocol involving two independent human raters and quadratic-weighted kappa to assess inter-rater agreement and support future validation of AI-generated scores. Overall, the findings demonstrate the feasibility of transparent, rubric-based AI-assisted oral assessment while emphasizing measurement limitations, standardized expert ratings, and human oversight.

items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly embedded in higher education learning practices, yet its contribution to academic performance remains contested. This study developed an explainable machine-learning framework for predicting students’ post-semester GPA from Generative AI usage patterns and learning-related characteristics. Using a structured dataset of 50,000 student records, the study modelled academic performance with predictors including pre-semester GPA, weekly GenAI usage hours, primary use case, prompt-engineering skill, tool diversity, traditional study hours, perceived AI dependency, institutional policy, exam anxiety, year of study, and major category. To prevent outcome leakage, non-relevant outcome variables and student identifiers were excluded before training. Ridge Regression, Decision Tree Regression, and Extra Trees Regression were compared using R², RMSE, and MAE. The results showed that Ridge Regression achieved the strongest predictive performance, indicating that academic outcomes were largely explainable through stable relationships among prior achievement, GenAI-related behaviours, and study characteristics. items.title: Exploring general practitioners’ perceptions of the utility of AI-powered voice-to-text technology for clinical documentation during video consultations in Danish general practice: a qualitative study
items.abstract: Abstract Background Clinical documentation is crucial for maintaining continuity and quality of care; however, it has become increasingly time-consuming and complex in general practice, leading to administrative overload and burnout. Artificial intelligence-powered voice-to-text technologies (AIVT) have emerged as potential solutions to reduce this burden by automatically transcribing and organizing consultations into clinical notes. This study assesses perceptions of the utility of an AIVT tool for clinical documentation during video consultations. Methods A qualitative study was conducted using triangulation of observations, think-aloud sessions, and semi-structured interviews. A total of 18 general practitioners from 14 clinics across all five Danish regions tested Autonotar, a use case for an AIVT tool that generates draft clinical notes during video consultations. Data were analyzed deductively using predefined criteria: demand, acceptability, and perceived future efficacy. Results The findings indicate: (1) structural drivers of demand show how increasing regulatory and defensive documentation pressures create a perceived need for technological support; (2) conditions for acceptable use highlight where general practitioners emphasize the importance of clinical accuracy, alignment with workflow, and robust data protection; and (3) perceived future value demonstrates how participants view AIVT as a way to reduce administrative workload, improve work-life balance, and enhance patient engagement—provided the tool delivers reliable output and is responsibly integrated into clinical systems. Conclusions Based on the study use case, AIVT may offer a practical means of supporting clinical documentation in Danish general practice, but its utility is conditional rather than inherent. GPs expressed cautious optimism about its potential to reduce documentation burden, improve work–life balance, and support patient engagement. However, adoption will depend on reliable output, workflow integration, clear accountability, robust data protection, and adaptation to different consultation modalities. Sustainable implementation requires technological maturity and sociotechnical alignment among clinicians, decision-makers, and technology providers.

items.title: EXPLORING PHYSIOTHERAPIST MOVEMENT DURING PATIENT AND THERAPEUTIC HANDLING IN A LABORATORY SETTING
items.abstract: Conflicts of Interest: No conflicts of interest Source of Funding: No funding obtained Background Back pain is the highest reported work-related musculoskeletal disorder among physiotherapists, frequently linked to patient handling. Neurological rehabilitation often requires sustained forward-flexed and asymmetrical postures, yet objective biomechanical evidence describing whole body and inter-segmental spinal movement during therapeutic handling is limited. This study aimed to evaluate the feasibility of capturing neurological patient handling tasks in a motion-capture laboratory and explore how physiotherapist positioning (standing, sitting front/side, half-kneeling) influences postural injury risk during two handling tasks. Methods A two-phase observational laboratory study using Vicon motion capture was conducted. A feasibility phase with physiotherapy students assessed data quality and participant-acceptability. Two tasks were then examined in a pilot study with qualified neurological physiotherapists and volunteers with neurological conditions. Inter-segmental spinal (lumbar, thoracic, cervical), shoulder, hip and knee kinematics were quantified during sit-to-stand and supine lower-limb gait facilitation tasks performed from varied positions. Time-normalised kinematic data were analysed using Rapid Upper Limb Assessment and Postural Load Index frameworks to determine risk. Results Sustained thoracic flexion was consistently observed, exceeding ergonomic thresholds for increased injury risk. Physiotherapist positioning significantly influenced movement patterns; no single position reduced exposure across all body regions, instead redistributing postural demands between the spinal segments and shoulders. Inter-segmental analysis revealed regional differences in spinal injury risk that may be underestimated by tools treating the trunk as a single segment. Conclusion Varying physiotherapist position redistributed biomechanical demand, offering options to modify handling techniques. Integrating inter-segmental biomechanical analysis with ergonomic assessment could offer clinically relevant insights to inform physiotherapy-specific training and back pain prevention strategies.

items.title: Exploring the moderating role of pain coping strategies on the association between work-related physical and psychosocial factors and musculoskeletal disorders in healthcare workers
items.abstract: Background Musculoskeletal disorders (MSDs) are highly prevalent among healthcare workers due to the physical and psychosocial demands of their job. These conditions lead to significant functional limitations and impose a substantial economic burden. Objective This study aimed to investigate whether pain coping strategies moderate the relationship between work-related physical and psychosocial factors and MSDs. Methods A cross-sectional study was conducted among 130 healthcare workers at Northwest General Hospital, Peshawar, Pakistan. Data were analyzed using SPSS version 27 and moderation analysis was performed using the PROCESS macro version 4.2 by Andrew F. Hayes. Results Strong positive correlations were found between pain coping strategies and neck-shoulder pain (r = 0.86, p < 0.001) and upper extremity pain (r = 0.65, p < 0.001), while a weaker correlation was observed with low back pain (r = 0.34, p < 0.001). Work-related psychosocial and physical factors were strongly associated with neck, shoulder, and upper extremity pain, while their relationship with low back pain was moderate. Moderation analysis showed that pain coping strategies significantly moderated the relationship between work demands and neck-shoulder pain ( p = 0.00182). Similarly, coping strategies moderated the effect of heavy physical load on upper extremity pain ( p = 0.0195). However, no significant moderating effect was found for low back pain. Conclusion Pain coping strategies significantly moderate the relationship between work-related physical and psychosocial factors and MSDs, particularly in the neck, shoulder, and upper extremities. These findings suggest that integrating coping-based interventions into occupational health programs may help mitigate the burden of MSDs among healthcare workers.

items.title: Fairness or Fallacy? Mapping the Landscape of AI Bias in Disease Detection
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has several transformative effects on healthcare, like to facilitate clinicians in disease detection and to manage patient care with enhanced precision. Due to the increasing complexity of medical data and the growing volume of diagnostic images, the substantial computational power needed to process such information creates both opportunities and challenges. To accomplish this objective, numerous methodologies have been proposed to integrate AI into disease detection systems. All these methodologies consider different aspects of clinical diagnosis, considering key parameters such as the type of AI model employed, the nature of input data, and the population demographics being analysed. In this paper, we review different state-of-the-art techniques which have been proposed for various areas of disease detection, specifically focusing on bias identification and mitigation. The proposed solutions are distinguished based on the type of input data they utilize, the architecture of model, and type of bias (algorithmic bias, demographic bias, model bias, and deployment bias). The time frame chosen to filter out relevant studies is between 2015 and 2026. Eventually, we review 23 related articles out of 64,389 analyzed from seven different digital libraries. The obtained results guide us to reach a conclusion with respect to state-of-the-art selected studies. Furthermore, these results reveal significant research gaps that can assist researchers in addressing AI-related bias in medical diagnosis. By prioritizing explainability, data diversity, and fairness in algorithmic design, as well as equitable access for affected patient populations, they can utilize available healthcare resources more effectively.

items.title: Fake News, Real Crashes: Information Injection Attacks on LLM Financial Trading Agents
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents now trade real capital using news as evidence, yet they cannot reliably tell fabricated headlines from real news. Because they read the same feeds under near-identical policies, a single fabricated post can push them into the same trade at the same moment. We present a systematic attack benchmark for information injection against LLM trading agents. Unlike prompt injection, which targets the model's instructions, information injection targets the evidence the agent trusts. The benchmark spans five injection vectors and seven event categories, evaluated over ~10,000 decisions on 15 U.S. stocks. Five findings emerge. (i) Prompt injection achieves 14% attack success rate (ASR), but fabricated news reaches 62% and two 30-word templates reach 100% on all 15 stocks, inverting the usual LLM-security intuition. (ii) For fact-poisoning templates, surface form matters more than content, since removing credibility cues such as a named source or a "BREAKING" tag drops ASR from 100% to 0% while the fake claim remains identical. (iii) Success depends on the agent's state, with a fake indicator panel scoring 91% against an agent about to hold but 12% against one about to buy. (iv) Attacks generalize across model vendors and remain effective when blended, unlabeled, into real news feeds. (v) Most attacks evade standard defenses, since model scaling stops shallow vectors but not fact poisoning, peer debate fails, and only hierarchical aggregation reduces ASR.

items.title: Financial time-series generation: a systematic survey of taxonomy, evaluation, datasets, and open challenges
items.abstract: The rapid advancement of generative artificial intelligence has catalyzed a paradigm shift in quantitative finance, transitioning from traditional point forecasting toward comprehensive financial time-series generation (FTSG) across extrapolation, imputation, and full-scale data synthesis. This transition is motivated by the critical need to simulate rare market regimes, reconstruct incomplete historical records, and produce privacy-preserving synthetic environments for stress testing and trading execution. However, empirical financial properties—including heavy tails, volatility clustering, non-stationarity, and regime shifts—pose severe hurdles for generic generative frameworks. In this systematic survey, we review 131 studies from 2021 to early 2026 to bridge the gap between machine learning capabilities and econometric validity. We introduce a two-level taxonomy structuring the domain across task formulations and algorithmic families, and establish a multi-dimensional evaluation protocol encompassing distributional fidelity, stylized facts preservation, and downstream utility. Furthermore, we catalog curated financial databases and benchmark suites while addressing empirical dataset construction pitfalls. Finally, we identify pivotal open challenges in causal representation learning, econometrically bounded modeling, and online adaptation under distribution shifts. This review provides a standardized roadmap for developing robust, domain-aligned financial generative models.

items.title: FinHopper: A Progressive Multi-Hop Benchmark for Complex Financial Agents with Step-wise Evaluation
items.abstract: Financial agents are expected to answer factual investment queries through open search, but financial multi-hop retrieval differs from general multi-hop QA in a crucial way: each intermediate answer is an exact typed constraint, such as an entity, date, event, or numerical indicator, that determines the next query. This strict answer-conditioned dependency makes small intermediate errors cascade into plausible but wrong search trajectories. We introduce FinHopper, a benchmark for complex financial agents with controlled reasoning depth from 1 to 6 hops, covering stocks, funds, and macroeconomic facts, with gold intermediate answers for process-level evaluation. To construct FinHopper at scale, we design a state-transition-based synthesis framework that composes verified atomic financial QA patterns into dependency-preserving chains, followed by targeted in-synthesis verification, model-ensemble checking, and public-search validation by financial experts. Experiments with 20 LLM-agent configurations show that public search tools are necessary but insufficient: performance drops sharply as hop depth increases, the best model remains far below human experts, and process-aware scoring reveals partial reasoning progress hidden by final-answer-only evaluation. The benchmark is available at https://github.com/justajustin/FinHopper/.

items.title: FinSafeGuard: A Quality-Driven Synthetic Dataset for Financial AI Safety
items.abstract: Generating high-quality synthetic datasets at scale remains a fundamental challenge for training specialized AI systems in data-scarce domains. We present a comprehensive methodology that produces 14.3 million quality-filtered synthetic training examples from a structured taxonomy of 632,000 scenario specifications. Our four-stage pipeline ad- dresses critical challenges in synthetic data quality, diversity, and realism through: (1) systematic pre-generation research establishing optimal generation parameters via diminishing returns analysis, (2) conditional auto evolution mechanisms that remediate low-diversity batches during generation, (3) a two-layer semantic deduplication architecture combining lexical and embedding-based methods, and (4) LLM-as-Judge quality evaluation filtering samples based on behavioral correctness and tuple fidelity. Empirical analysis across three domains (Banking, Insurance, Financial Services) demonstrates domain-specific deduplication patterns ranging from 9.9% to 40.6%, with output generation modes exhibiting highest redundancy. Our batch size optimization reveals mode-specific diversity saturation thresholds, enabling principled allocation strategies. The complete pipeline reduces 26.4M raw samples to 14.3M high-confidence examples through merge (20.9% reduction), semantic deduplication (18.7% reduction), and quality-based filtering (15.9% reduction), providing a reproducible framework for domain-specific synthetic data generation with rigorous quality control.

items.title: ForagerSim: Evaluating Embodied Map-Based Reasoning in Large-Scale Dynamic Worlds
items.abstract: Animals build cognitive maps of vast environments, use them to perform map-based navigation, and might even be reusing the same circuitry used in spatial reasoning for creating and using maps of arbitrary task-spaces. In contrast, current embodied AI systems either rely on hand-engineered mapping pipelines, which break in the presence of unmodeled dynamics and are restricted to metric space, or on learned policies that rarely form map-like representations at all. Developing architectures that could learn to build and use map-like representations as flexibly as animals is, however, difficult because few embodied AI benchmarks actually require map-based reasoning. To address this, we present ForagerSim --- an interdisciplinary research platform and simulation environment focused on embodied tasks that require map-based reasoning, with scenarios ranging from mobile-robot search and rescue to animal foraging in both complex mazes and vast, potentially infinite open areas. ForagerSim is highly modular and allows modifying independent axes of difficulty related to perception (abstract 2D sensing to full RGB or LiDAR), scale (room-scale to multi-km scale), topology (open-fields to complex mazes), dynamics (smoke, debris, sensorimotor failures and others) and tasks (from simple 2D coverage to foraging-inspired well-alternation tasks). We compare reinforcement learning baselines with a simple engineered robotics stack and a human player on 8 example worlds which show how different difficulty axes affect existing methods. Our results show that, when sensing is simplified to 2D, learned policies can perform multi-object search and well-alternation tasks surprisingly well in simple topologies, but they fall short of human performance in larger or more complex-topology environments where map-based baselines perform well, suggesting that map-based reasoning is the bottleneck in these scenarios.

items.title: FrameGRPO: Incentivizing Video Reasoning via Multi-Frame Rollouts and Temporal Credit
items.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, particularly Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), has improved video reasoning in multimodal large language models. However, standard video GRPO varies only linguistic trajectories while conditioning every rollout in a group on the same sampled frames, which can produce homogeneous rewards and weaken group-relative learning when the shared visual evidence is insufficient or distracting. We propose \textbf{FrameGRPO}, a simple and effective reinforcement-learning framework that requires neither auxiliary networks nor changes to the model architecture. Specifically, FrameGRPO combines two lightweight components: (1) \textbf{Multi-Frame Rollouts}, which use only uniform temporal subsampling of a single maximal-frame decode to construct aligned views that diversify visual evidence and reasoning trajectories; and (2) \textbf{Gated Temporal Efficiency Credit}, which selectively reinforces a correct lower-ratio trajectory when all rollouts in a fixed full-ratio reference subset fail, without imposing an unconditional preference for fewer frames. Extensive experiments across diverse video understanding and reasoning benchmarks demonstrate robust overall improvements over standard GRPO, highlighting temporal-view diversification as an effective mechanism for exploration and credit assignment in video MLLMs.

items.title: FraudShield AI: Machine Learning for Credit Card Fraud Detection Under Severe Class Imbalance
items.abstract: FraudShield AI is a machine-learning project designed to identify potentially fraudulent credit card transactions using artificial intelligence. Built with Python, scikit-learn, pandas, and Streamlit, the application uses a Random Forest classification model to analyze transaction data and distinguish between legitimate and potentially fraudulent activity. It features an interactive dashboard for exploring transaction records, checking individual transactions, visualizing model performance, and examining feature importance. Through this project, I gained practical experience in machine learning, data analysis, model evaluation, and application development while exploring the challenges of imbalanced datasets and responsible AI. FraudShield AI reflects my interest in combining artificial intelligence and cybersecurity to develop practical solutions for financial security.

items.title: From Authorship to Accountability - Rethinking Copyright Governance for AI-Generated Art
items.abstract: This study examines how the rapid expansion of generative artificial intelligence (AI) challenges traditional copyright law by shifting legal concerns beyond authorship and ownership toward transparency, disclosure, traceability, and accountability in AI-assisted artistic production.The study adopts a doctrinal and comparative legal methodology to analyse copyright principles, emerging regulatory frameworks, and policy developments relating to AI-generated content. Particular attention is given to the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act, international copyright debates, and the Albanian legal framework under Law No. 35/2016 “On Copyright and Related Rights”.The analysis demonstrates that existing copyright regimes remain predominantly authorship-centred and provide limited guidance regarding accountability when AI systems contribute to artistic creation. Significant regulatory gaps persist concerning disclosure obligations, traceability of AI involvement, transparency of creative processes, and the allocation of responsibility among users, developers, and platform providers. The findings further indicate that accountabilitybased governance offers a valuable complement to traditional copyright doctrines in addressing the challenges of AI-assisted creativity. The study is limited to legal JUS & JUSTICIA No. 20, ISSUE 2/ 2026 95 and regulatory analysis and does not incorporate empirical evidence from creators, policymakers, technology developers, or judicial practice in Albania. Future research may benefit from examining stakeholder perspectives and the practical implementation of emerging AI governance frameworks. The findings support the development of governance mechanisms based on mandatory disclosure of AI involvement, documentation of human creative contribution, enhanced transparency standards, and traceability measures for AI-generated artistic content. These measures may strengthen legal certainty and improve copyright enforcement in AIassisted creative environments.The study contributes to current scholarship by moving beyond the traditional debate on authorship and copyrightability and proposing an accountability-oriented framework for copyright governance. It offers one of the first analyses linking transparency, disclosure, traceability, and accountability principles to the regulation of AI-generated art within both the Albanian and European legal contexts.

items.title: From Black Box to Controller: Inference-Time Steering of LLM via Feature Amplification
items.abstract: Inference-time steering is crucial for deploying Large Language Models (LLMs) in real-world applications, where they must flexibly adjust behavior preferences. For instance, a model should dynamically adjust its caution level based on the risk of the scenario. This requirement introduces a challenge: modulating the intensity of LLM preferences. Prompt engineering can require task-specific prompt design, while fine-tuning requires additional optimization and data. These requirements can make repeated behavioral adjustments costly. To address this, we introduce NeuroSteer, a plug-and-play framework that enables flexible, quantitative adjustment of LLM preferences at inference time. NeuroSteer employs a Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) as its controller. Comparing neuron activation frequencies between positive and negative examples isolates "feature neurons" that correspond to target preferences such as politeness and positive sentiment. During inference, the activations of selected SAE features are amplified in the latent representations to steer the output distribution. Users can adjust the strength of this steering on a per-scenario or per-user basis, granting the LLM fine-grained, quantifiable trait modulation. Our experiments show that NeuroSteer can alter sentiment, toxicity, stance, and politeness at inference time. It achieves higher target-direction steering scores than the compared baselines in several settings, with task- and strength-dependent trade-offs in generation quality.

items.title: From Chaos to Consistency: A Human-Centered Framework for AI-supported Assessment at a Mission-Driven Liberal Arts College
items.abstract: This practitioner inquiry reports on a pilot at a small Catholic liberal arts college that used generative artificial intelligence (GenAI)-supported tools to help faculty complete program-assessment documentation during a structured Education Day. Grounded in Catholic social teaching and human-centered AI principles, the pilot tested a framework organized around human judgment, ethical stewardship, and formative human-AI partnership. Survey results from the pilot cohort (N = 10; item-level valid responses varied) showed strong faculty endorsement, including unanimous agreement that the process deepened thinking about evidence of student learning and unanimous intent to use AI-supported tools in future cycles. Qualitative findings identified five themes: efficiency and cognitive scaffolding, human-in-the-loop validation, platform reliability and trust, data governance, and institutional support infrastructure. Findings suggest that mission-driven institutions can integrate AI into assessment responsibly when faculty formation, verification checkpoints, and governance structures precede broad implementation.

items.title: From Choice to Consequence: Active Resilience as the Value-Adding Extension of the Next? Path and Pattern of Personal and Business Innovation Practice
items.abstract: The research previously conducted by Benjamin and McLaughlin (2026) defined applied curiosity as the governing architecture for the transition from artificial intelligence (AI) to augmented understanding (AU), and presented cCC* (Curiosity opening Chances, discriminating Choices, authorising Changes) as its compact engine. That account stopped at authorisation. It did not address what happens when an authorised Change is enacted, meets resistance, produces an unintended consequence, or is overtaken by a shifting environment. Once change is enacted, subsequent Curiosity is enabled and thus the mechanism becomes recursive. This article develops active resilience (AR) as an extension of that research, serving as the architecture that governs that remainder and connecting Artificial Intelligence (AI), Applied Curiosity (AC), Augmented Understanding (AU) and Active Resilience (AR) into the sequence AI -> AC -> AU -> AR -> NEXT?: not the capacity to return to a prior state, but the capacity to enact a provisional best fit choice, detect its consequences, and use the resulting difference to reconstruct the next state. AR is defined against four guardrails: BBBB (the Belonging, Becoming, Bridging and Building movements applied at the point of action as a viability guardrail over bodily, behavioural, relational and environmental boundaries), FFFF (Form, Function, Frame and Future: whether an action responds to the form and function of the situation rather than merely to the frame placed over it, and what futures it opens or forecloses), the P-M-Theta-Phi test (practicable, methodically warranted, theoretically coherent, value explicit), and a feedback discipline that returns consequence to renewed curiosity rather than reinforcing the original construction. The framework is grounded in established literatures, including Holling's distinction between engineering and ecological resilience and his four-phase adaptive cycle of growth, conservation, release and reorganisation. Holling's work is particularly relevant to AR because it challenges the assumption that resilience is achieved by holding a system in a linear, stable state; attempts to suppress variability and maintain tight control can instead reduce adaptive capacity, accumulate fragility and increase the probability of eventual system disruption. AR also draws on Argyris and Schon's account of single-loop and double-loop organisational learning, Weick's concept of enactment, and von Bertalanffy's general systems account of equifinality. Within this literature, cCC* is positioned as an operational synthesis: a repeatable mechanism for translating these principles into the ongoing processes of inquiry, discrimination, action and adaptation. It extends the R1-R16 transitional register introduced previously, reading it this time as an architecture of choice under AEIOUF (Agency, Environment, Identity, Options, Understanding, Futures). A conceptual method for AR enactment and sixteen accompanying research propositions are offered for organisational strategy, stakeholder engagement, public narrative and reflective governance. The central claim is that an AU relationship is not complete at the moment a decision is authorised. It is complete only when the organisation or person can act on that decision, absorb what the action reveals, and remain capable of choosing again. MORE, in this account, is not a state reached once but a capacity kept renewable.

items.title: From chronic kidney disease classification to genuine early prediction: a systematic review of artificial intelligence, methodological quality, and translational evidence
items.abstract: Introduction Artificial intelligence has been widely applied to chronic kidney disease (CKD), but the term ‘prediction” is frequently used for tasks ranging from contemporaneous disease classification to genuine forecasting of future renal outcomes. This systematic review examined this distinction while evaluating methodological quality and evidence for clinical translation. Methods A predefined Scopus-based search covering 2021–2026 identified eligible AI- and machine-learning-based CKD studies. After screening and duplicate reconciliation, 169 unique primary studies were included. Future-oriented prediction required an identifiable baseline, predictors available at or before baseline, a subsequent renal outcome, and a meaningful prediction horizon. Studies were evaluated for modeling approaches, datasets, validation, calibration, explainability, clinical usefulness, and methodological quality using PROBAST+AI. Results Of 169 studies, 122 (72.2%) addressed current-state CKD detection or classification, while only 46 (27.2%) contained a clearly future-oriented prediction component. Seventeen studies used geographic or institutional external validation and only four used an independent external cohort or dataset. Calibration was assessed in 12 studies and explicit explainability methods were reported in 16. PROBAST+AI identified high overall risk of bias in 156 studies during development and 164 during evaluation, with no study achieving an overall low-risk judgement. Discussion CKD-AI evidence is substantially stronger for retrospective classification than for genuine early prediction or clinical translation. Future research should prioritize longitudinal prediction, independent and temporal validation, leakage-resistant analysis, calibration, clinically validated explainability, and prospective real-world evaluation.

items.title: From Cities to Distributed Intelligence Landscapes: Hybrid Foresight Through Drawing, Philosophy, and Generative AI
items.abstract: This research investigates an alternative approach to long-range urban foresight by employing a hybrid methodology combining deep-time conceptual reflection, exploratory drawing as an epistemic practice, structured interpretative analysis, and AI-assisted dialogical synthesis. The resulting synthesis articulates a theoretically generated post-urban scenario characterized by dispersed human habitation embedded in ecological landscapes, supported by advanced digital connectivity and artificial intelligence. Technologically intensive functions remain concentrated in infrastructural hubs, while everyday life becomes integrated with natural environments through walking-based mobility, bio-inspired architecture, and multispecies coexistence. The proposed model reinterprets urbanity as distributed intelligence within ecological continuity.
