items.title: From Co-Presence to Willingness to Pay More: How Remote Guidance Service and Embodied Action Simulation Drive Brand Value in the Virtual Environments
items.abstract: This study investigates how perceived co-presence contributes to brand value in virtual service environments. Drawing on Mirror Neuron Theory and Embodied Knowledge Theory, we propose embodied action simulation as an indirect path linking perceived co-presence to brand image and subsequent willingness to pay more. We further conceptualize remote guidance service as a service-design boundary condition and compare AI- versus human-delivered guidance from a task-agent fit perspective. Three studies (two laboratory studies in Roblox Vans World and a field survey of smart fitness mirror users) support the framework. Embodied action simulation mediates the relationship between perceived co-presence and brand image, while this indirect association is stronger when remote guidance service is present. A stronger indirect association is also observed among AI-coach than human-coach users in procedural, task-oriented service contexts, consistent with task-agent fit. These findings clarify how social presence relates to embodied participation, brand value creation, and consumers’ willingness to pay more.

items.title: From few‐shot learning to data‐efficient intelligence
items.abstract: Abstract Modern artificial intelligence (AI) has achieved remarkable progress by scaling data, model size, and computation. Yet scaling alone does not resolve one of the most fundamental gaps between machine and human intelligence: the ability to learn, adapt, and act from limited experience. This limitation is especially visible when labeled examples, expert feedback, user interactions, or real‐world trials are scarce, costly, or dynamically changing. Humans can often grasp a new concept, adapt to a new goal, or personalize behavior after only a few examples or interactions, but many AI systems remain fragile under the same conditions. My research studies data‐efficient generalization: how learning systems can acquire useful priors, adapt to new tasks, and reuse limited experience under bounded supervision. In this article, I trace a continuous research path from few‐shot learning to meta‐learning, in‐context learning, and data‐efficient agentic learning. I first revisit few‐shot learning as a foundational problem and explain how data‐, model‐, and algorithm‐level priors make learning possible when empirical risk minimization is unreliable. I then describe our work on meta‐learning, where task‐level information and parameter‐efficient adaptation enable fast generalization. Next, I discuss in‐context learning in large language models (LLMs) as an implicit form of learning to learn, and show how its connection to classical meta‐learning provides both theoretical insight and practical guidance. Finally, I turn to large language model (LLM)‐based agents, where data efficiency expands beyond labels to include demonstrations, reasoning traces, tool‐use records, preferences, memory, and feedback. Across AI for science, biomedical knowledge discovery, recommendation, search, and personalization, the common thread is simple: more capable AI should extract more learning signal from less experience.

items.title: From GEMBA to GPT: Artificial Intelligence for the Medical Office Assistant
items.abstract: Administrative tasks by medical office staff are a significant but underappreciated driver of delayed patient care, staff burnout, and escalating operational costs in modern urology practice. A forced Gemba Walk in front-desk responsibilities exposed many previously invisible inefficiencies in my own practice, specifically the workflow with regard to faxes and patient phone calls. These tasks are high-volume, redundant, and time-consuming—making them an ideal task for artificial intelligence (AI). Large language models (LLM) can integrate with electronic medical record (EMR) platforms to automate these repetitive tasks. For example, optical character recognition (OCR) can be used to transform incoming faxed images to operational datapoints. The models can then automatically classify the document, sort the file directly to patient charts, and clinically triage referrals and results by urgency. Furthermore, AI voice agents or AI receptionists can handle routine phone calls with full EMR integration and documentation, while complex cases can be escalated to human staff. In an era of increasing burnout, transitioning from manual workflows to an AI-augmented paradigm allows providers to work at the top of their scope. These operational efficiencies carry broader health policy implications, including shortened referral-to-consultation intervals for urgent diagnoses, improved patient care and communication, and the generation of structured analytics to drive system-level quality improvement.

items.title: From Heuristics to Learning a Review of AI Methods for Logic Gate in EDA
items.abstract: Description This review paper examines how Artificial Intelligence is changing logic gate synthesis in Electronic Design Automation (EDA). Classical heuristics such as Karnaugh maps, Quine-McCluskey and AIG rewriting struggle to scale to circuits with billions of gates, especially when balancing power, performance and area (PPA). The paper builds on Astillero's study of AI-driven synthesis and organizes the field around three model families: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs): these represent circuits as directed graphs and estimate delay, power and congestion before physical routing. Reinforcement Learning (RL): agents learn sequences of rewrite operations on And-Inverter Graphs (AIGs) and Majority-Inverter Graphs (MIGs) that greedy optimizers miss, guided by a combined area, delay and power reward. Large Circuit Models (LCMs): transformer models that translate specifications or HDL directly into gate-level netlists. The paper compares these methods with traditional flows across five dimensions: optimization strategy, PPA exploration, scaling, parasitic awareness and adaptability across technology libraries. It then covers three applications: approximate computing, SAT sweeping and equivalence checking, and automated CPU/ASIC generation. It concludes that data scarcity and the lack of guaranteed functional correctness are the main barriers to adoption. It argues that closing the loop between generation and formal verification is the key research priority.
